docs.title: AutoAgentAI
docs.text:
AutoAgent and Customer-Integrated Custom Insights into Purchase and Overall Behaviour and Decision Making.

One-line definition

AutoAgentAI is an autonomous AI agent that unifies a business's customer data and continuously produces custom insights into how customers buy, behave, and decide — then surfaces or acts on those insights to improve decisions.

Focus: automotive, on-prem, private

The beachhead is the car industry — dealerships and, through them, OEMs — where the buyer's pre-purchase decision behaviour is the most valuable, least-captured data there is. AutoAgentAI is built to run on-prem on local AI models, so sensitive customer data never leaves the building. See Deployment & Privacy and the Perspectives articles.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Businesses sit on fragmented customer data — transactions, web and app events, CRM records, support tickets, reviews, campaign responses. The signal about why customers buy, how they behave, and how they decide is spread across those silos and mostly goes unread. Static dashboards answer yesterday's questions and wait for a human to ask the next one.

AutoAgentAI replaces "dashboard you have to drive" with "agent that drives itself": it integrates the data, keeps looking, generates insights tailored to each business and customer, and turns them into recommended or automated actions.

docs.title: The AutoAgent Loop
docs.text: Pillar 5. The orchestrator that makes the system an agent rather than a pipeline. It holds goals, decides what to do next, invokes the other pillars as tools, remembers, and acts within guardrails.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    PERCEIVE[Perceive<br/><small>read state, data, goals</small>] --> REASON[Reason & plan<br/><small>what matters, what to do</small>]
    REASON --> ACT[Act<br/><small>run tools, recommend, execute</small>]
    ACT --> LEARN[Learn<br/><small>observe outcomes, update memory</small>]
    LEARN --> PERCEIVE

Unlike a dashboard that waits for a query, the AutoAgent runs this loop on its own cadence — scheduled, event-triggered, or on demand — and chooses its own next question.

docs.title: Perceive
docs.text: Read current goals, recent data and events from the integration layer, outputs from the behaviour models, and its own memory of what it has already done and learned.

docs.title: Reason & plan
docs.text: Decide what matters now and form a plan: which segments or customers to look at, which insights to pursue, which decisions to prepare. This is where goals and priorities shape attention.

docs.title: Act
docs.text: Invoke pillars 1–4 as tools, surface insights, propose or (within guardrails) execute actions. Every act is recorded with its reasoning.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text: Observe outcomes (via attribution), update memory and the sense of what works, and feed results back to the models. The next loop is better-informed than the last.

docs.title: The agent as a tool-user
docs.text:
The AutoAgent doesn't reimplement the pillars — it calls them, plus the business's systems, as tools:

flowchart TB
    AG(["AutoAgent<br/>plan · decide · remember"])
    AG --> Q[Query unified data]
    AG --> M[Run / read behaviour models]
    AG --> I[Generate insights]
    AG --> D[Produce decisions]
    AG --> X[Execute actions in business systems]
    Q -.results.-> AG
    M -.results.-> AG
    I -.results.-> AG
    D -.results.-> AG
    X -.outcomes.-> AG

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The agent is stateful. Memory makes it improve and keeps it from repeating itself:

Memory type Holds Used for Working The current investigation's context Completing the task at hand Episodic Past insights, actions, and their outcomes Not re-surfacing known findings; learning what worked Semantic Durable knowledge about the business, its customers, and its goals Grounding reasoning in context

docs.title: Guardrails and autonomy levels
docs.text:
Autonomy is configurable and graduated. Guardrails define what the agent may do on its own.

flowchart LR
    L0["L0 · Observe<br/><small>insights only</small>"] --> L1["L1 · Recommend<br/><small>proposes, human acts</small>"]
    L1 --> L2["L2 · Act w/ approval<br/><small>one-click human gate</small>"]
    L2 --> L3["L3 · Act within limits<br/><small>auto if low-stakes + confident</small>"]
    L3 --> L4["L4 · Autonomous<br/><small>auto within broad guardrails</small>"]

Typical guardrails:

  • Stakes & reversibility — irreversible or high-cost actions require approval.
  • Confidence floors — act only above a confidence threshold.
  • Budget & frequency caps — spend and contact limits per customer/segment.
  • Excluded actions & audiences — hard "never do this" rules.
  • Escalation — anything outside the envelope is escalated to a human.

A business starts low (observe/recommend) and raises autonomy per action type as the agent earns trust through its track record.

docs.title: Safety and accountability
docs.text:
• Full audit trail — every perception, decision, and action is logged with reasoning and provenance.
  • Explainability on demand — any output can be traced back to its evidence.
  • Reversibility & kill-switch — actions are reversible where possible, and the agent can be paused instantly.
  • Resistant to bad input — the agent treats external/customer-supplied text as data, not instructions, and validates surprising signals before acting.

docs.text:
• The agent framework / reasoning model and how planning is implemented.
  • Cadence: schedule, event triggers, and how continuous "continuous" is.
  • Exact memory representation and retention.
  • Default guardrail envelopes shipped out of the box.

docs.title: Cross-cutting concerns
docs.text:
These apply to every pillar and must be designed in, not bolted on:

  • Trust & provenance — every insight and action carries a trace from raw data through reasoning to output, enabling explanation and audit.
  • Privacy & consent — identity resolution and action-taking respect consent, data-minimization, and regional rules (e.g. GDPR/CCPA). Covered further in Customer Integration.
  • Guardrails & autonomy level — what the agent may do without approval is explicit and configurable. See The AutoAgent Loop.
  • Observability — the system's own behaviour (what it looked at, decided, and did) is logged and measurable.
  • Extensibility — new data sources, models, and action types plug in without reworking the core.

docs.title: Design stance (intentionally not yet decided)
docs.text: This document describes the logical architecture. The physical choices — languages, model providers, datastores, deployment — are deliberately deferred to the specifications so the concept isn't prematurely locked to a stack. Where a choice is load-bearing, it will be recorded as a decision with trade-offs when specs begin.

docs.title: Behaviour Models
docs.text:
Pillar 3. The quantitative understanding of customers: how they purchase, how they behave overall, and where they are in their journey. These models feed the Insights Engine and Decision Intelligence.

flowchart LR
    UP[(Unified profiles<br/>+ events)] --> PUR[Purchase behaviour]
    UP --> OVR[Overall behaviour]
    UP --> JRN[Journey / lifecycle]
    PUR --> OUT[Segments · propensities · drivers]
    OVR --> OUT
    JRN --> OUT

docs.title: Purchase behaviour
docs.text:
How customers buy — the commercial core.

Model / measure Question it answers RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) How recently, often, and valuably does this customer buy? Purchase propensity How likely is this customer to buy (soon / this product)? Basket / affinity What products are bought together or in sequence? Price sensitivity How does this customer respond to price and promotions? LTV / CLV What is this customer worth over their lifetime? Churn / lapse risk How likely is this customer to stop buying?

docs.title: Overall behaviour
docs.text:
The relationship beyond the transaction — often the leading indicator of purchase behaviour.

Model / measure Question it answers Engagement score How actively is the customer interacting (visits, usage, opens)? Feature / product usage What are they using, how deeply, and is it growing? Support & satisfaction How much friction are they hitting; how do they feel? Sentiment What is the tone of their feedback and interactions? Channel preference Where and how do they prefer to engage?

docs.title: Behavioural segmentation
docs.text:
Rather than fixed demographic buckets, customers are grouped by how they behave, and segments are re-learned as behaviour shifts.

quadrantChart
    title Value vs. engagement (illustrative)
    x-axis Low engagement --> High engagement
    y-axis Low value --> High value
    quadrant-1 Champions
    quadrant-2 At-risk high-value
    quadrant-3 Low-priority
    quadrant-4 Growth potential

Segments are living: a customer can move between them, and the emergence of a new segment is itself an insight.

docs.title: Journey & lifecycle
docs.text:
Where a customer is in their arc, and what typically comes next.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Prospect
    Prospect --> New: first purchase
    New --> Active: repeat
    Active --> Loyal: sustained
    Active --> AtRisk: signals fade
    Loyal --> AtRisk: signals fade
    AtRisk --> Churned: lapse
    AtRisk --> Active: recovered
    Churned --> Reactivated: win-back
    Reactivated --> Active
    Churned --> [*]

Transitions carry probabilities and drivers, so the agent knows not just where a customer is but where they're heading and why.

docs.title: Modeling principles
docs.text:
1. Explainable first. Prefer models whose drivers can be surfaced; the Insights Engine needs the "why," not just the score.
  2. Features are shared. Behavioural features computed here are reused across models and insights, defined once in the integration layer.
  3. Honest uncertainty. Every prediction carries a confidence/interval; the agent treats a shaky prediction differently from a firm one.
  4. Monitored for drift. Behaviour changes; models are watched for decay and retrained, and drift is itself a signal.
  5. Start simple. Well-understood methods (RFM, logistic/propensity models, clustering) before complex ones — complexity is added only where it pays.

docs.title: Open questions (for specs)
docs.text:
• Which models are v1 (likely RFM, churn/purchase propensity, behavioural clustering) vs. later.
  • Build vs. buy for modeling infrastructure.
  • Training/serving cadence (batch scores vs. on-demand).
  • How model outputs are versioned so insights remain reproducible.

docs.title: Concepts & Glossary
docs.text: A shared vocabulary so the rest of the docs — and later the specs — mean the same thing by the same words.

docs.title: AutoAgent
docs.text: The autonomous orchestrator at the heart of the system. It holds goals, decides what to investigate, invokes the other components as tools, and chooses what to surface or act on. Distinguished from a passive report by initiative (it acts without being asked) and continuity (it runs on its own cadence). See The AutoAgent Loop.

docs.title: Customer-Integrated
docs.text: The property of being wired into a business's actual customer data and systems. Concretely: ingesting from the business's sources, resolving identities into one view per customer, and being able to read context and (eventually) trigger actions in those systems. See Customer Integration.

docs.title: Custom Insight
docs.text: A finding that is tailored (specific to this business / segment / customer), grounded (traceable to the data and reasoning behind it), and decision-oriented (it implies an action). Contrast with a generic benchmark or a raw metric. See Insights Engine.

docs.title: Purchase behaviour
docs.text: Everything about how a customer buys: what, when, how often, how much, through which channel, and in response to what. Includes conversion, basket composition, recency/frequency/monetary (RFM) patterns, price sensitivity, and churn.

docs.title: Overall behaviour
docs.text: The full relationship beyond transactions: engagement, product/feature usage, support interactions, content consumption, sentiment, and lifecycle stage. Purchase behaviour is a subset of overall behaviour.

docs.title: Decision Making
docs.text: The discipline of turning insight into action. In AutoAgentAI every insight is framed as a decision — a recommended next-best-action, a targeting choice, an intervention — with expected impact and a way to measure the result. See Decision Making.

docs.title: The five pillars
docs.text: # Pillar Role 1 Customer Integration Layer Connect, unify, resolve, and enrich customer data 2 Insights Engine Generate custom, grounded, decision-oriented insights 3 Behaviour Models Model purchase and overall behaviour (segments, propensities, journeys) 4 Decision Intelligence Turn insights into recommendations and actions 5 The AutoAgent Orchestrate the loop; hold goals, guardrails, and memory

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Term Definition Action A concrete step the agent recommends or takes (send offer, flag account, adjust segment). Attribution Measuring the outcome and impact caused by an action the agent took. CDP Customer Data Platform — a system that unifies customer data; AutoAgentAI can sit on one or provide its own integration layer. Churn A customer ending or lapsing their relationship (stopping purchases, cancelling). Cohort A group of customers sharing a defining trait or start time, analyzed together. Customer 360 / Unified profile One resolved record per customer combining all sources. Entity / Identity resolution Deciding that records across sources refer to the same customer. Feature (model sense) A computed signal about a customer used as model input (e.g. days-since-last-order). Guardrail A rule constraining what the agent may do autonomously (budget caps, approval gates, excluded actions). Human-in-the-loop (HITL) A person reviews/approves agent proposals before they take effect. Insight See Custom Insight. LTV / CLV (Customer) Lifetime Value — total value a customer is expected to generate. Next-best-action (NBA) The single most valuable action to take for a given customer right now. Propensity A modeled probability a customer will do something (buy, churn, upgrade). RFM Recency, Frequency, Monetary — a classic purchase-behaviour segmentation. Segment A defined group of customers sharing behaviour or attributes. Signal Any piece of customer data that may carry meaning. Tool (agent sense) A capability the agent can invoke — a query, a model, an API call. Trace / Provenance The recorded chain from raw data → reasoning → insight → action, enabling explanation and audit.

Naming discipline

When specs are written, terms defined here should be used verbatim. If a spec needs a new term, add it here first.

docs.title: Customer Integration Layer
docs.text:
Pillar 1. The foundation: turn fragmented, multi-source customer data into one trustworthy, resolved, enriched view per customer — and provide the read/write connection back to the business's systems.

Nothing downstream is better than this layer. Insights and decisions inherit the quality, coverage, and trustworthiness of the integration beneath them.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    ING[Ingest] --> NORM[Normalize] --> RES[Resolve identity] --> ENR[Enrich] --> STORE[(Store)]
    STORE --> SERVE[Serve to pillars 2–4]
    STORE --> ACT[Act back into sources]
  1. Ingest — pull/receive data from the business's sources.
  2. Normalize — map disparate schemas into a common model (customers, events, products, interactions).
  3. Resolve identity — decide which records across sources are the same person.
  4. Enrich — derive attributes and features (RFM, tenure, engagement scores).
  5. Store & serve — maintain unified profiles + event history for the other pillars.
  6. Act — provide the outbound connection so the agent can trigger actions (send a campaign, create a task, update a segment).

docs.title: Source taxonomy
docs.text:
Category Examples Typical signal Commerce / transactions Shopify, POS, billing, subscriptions What/when/how much bought CRM Salesforce, HubSpot Accounts, contacts, pipeline, notes Product / behavioural Web & app analytics, event streams Sessions, feature usage, clicks Support Zendesk, Intercom, tickets Issues, resolution, satisfaction Marketing Email, ads, campaign platforms Sends, opens, responses, spend Voice of customer Reviews, surveys, NPS Sentiment, verbatim feedback

Build vs. sit-on-top

AutoAgentAI can either provide this layer itself or sit on an existing CDP / data warehouse and consume its unified profiles. The architecture supports both; which to lead with is a go-to-market and spec decision (see roadmap).

docs.title: Identity resolution
docs.text:
The hardest and most valuable step: joining records that don't share a key.

flowchart TB
    R1[POS: email, card hash] --> M{Match}
    R2[CRM: email, phone, name] --> M
    R3[Analytics: device + email on login] --> M
    R4[Support: email, order #] --> M
    M -->|deterministic + probabilistic| UP[(Unified profile)]
    M -->|uncertain| REVIEW[Review / low-confidence link]
  • Deterministic matching on shared strong identifiers (email, phone, customer ID) first.
  • Probabilistic matching on weaker combinations (name + address, device + behaviour) with a confidence score.
  • Confidence-aware: low-confidence links are flagged rather than silently merged, because a bad merge corrupts every downstream insight.

docs.title: Privacy, consent, and trust
docs.text:
Customer data is sensitive and regulated. This layer is where those obligations are enforced:

  • Consent-aware: each profile records what the customer consented to; the agent may only use and act on data within that consent.
  • Data minimization: collect and retain only what's needed for the decisions being made.
  • Regional rules: support deletion/export requests and regional constraints (GDPR, CCPA, and similar).
  • Security: encryption in transit and at rest; least-privilege access; auditable access logs.
  • Provenance: every derived attribute records how and when it was computed, so downstream insights can be explained.

docs.title: Open questions (for specs)
docs.text:
• Real-time streaming vs. batch ingestion — and which sources need which.
  • Where unified profiles are materialized (own store vs. warehouse vs. CDP).
  • The exact match/merge policy and confidence thresholds.
  • How outbound actions are authorized and rate-limited per source.

docs.title: Decision Intelligence
docs.text:
Pillar 4. The last mile: turn insights and model outputs into decisions — specific recommendations and actions — and measure what they achieve.

This pillar is why the product exists. An insight that never changes a decision delivered no value. Here, every insight becomes a decision with an owner, an expected impact, and a way to tell whether it worked.

docs.title: From insight to decision
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    INS[Insight] --> OPT[Generate options]
    OPT --> SCORE[Score / simulate each]
    SCORE --> NBA[Next-best-action]
    NBA --> GATE{Within guardrails?}
    GATE -->|yes| ACT[Act automatically]
    GATE -->|no / high stakes| HITL[Recommend to human]
    HITL -->|approved| ACT
    ACT --> MEAS[Measure outcome]
    MEAS -->|attribution| LEARN[Feed back to models + agent]

docs.title: Next-best-action (NBA)
docs.text:
For a given customer or segment, the system determines the single most valuable action to take now, given goals, constraints, and predicted response.

Input Role Insight / propensity What's true and likely about the customer Action catalog The menu of possible actions (offer, message, flag, nurture…) Expected response Modeled effect of each action on this customer Goals & constraints What the business is optimizing and its limits (budget, frequency caps) Guardrails What's allowed autonomously vs. needs approval

The output is a ranked recommendation with the expected impact and the reasoning behind it — never an unexplained directive.

docs.title: Action catalog (illustrative)
docs.text:
Action Typical trigger Targeted offer / promotion High purchase propensity, price sensitivity known Retention / save play Rising churn risk on a valuable account Onboarding nudge Customer stalled at a known drop-off step Cross-/up-sell Affinity or usage signals readiness Flag for human High-stakes or low-confidence situation Segment / audience update Behavioural segment membership changed Suppress / do nothing Contact fatigue or no positive expected value

Doing nothing is a decision

Suppressing an action (to avoid fatigue or negative value) is a first-class output, not the absence of one.

docs.title: Measuring outcomes (attribution)
docs.text:
A decision isn't finished when the action fires — it's finished when its effect is measured and fed back.

  • Experimentation where feasible: holdouts / A-B tests so impact is causal, not just correlational.
  • Attribution: tie outcomes (purchase, retention, engagement lift) back to the action that drove them.
  • Learning loop: results update the behaviour models and the agent's sense of what works — so recommendations improve over time.
flowchart LR
    ACT[Action taken] --> OBS[Observe outcome]
    OBS --> ATTR[Attribute impact<br/>vs. holdout]
    ATTR --> MODELS[Update behaviour models]
    ATTR --> AGENT[Update agent policy]
    MODELS --> BETTER[Better next-best-actions]
    AGENT --> BETTER

docs.title: Human-in-the-loop and trust
docs.text:
Autonomy is graduated (see guardrails):

  • Low-stakes, high-confidence, reversible actions → the agent may act automatically.
  • High-stakes, low-confidence, or costly actions → the agent recommends, a human approves.
  • Every decision — auto or approved — is logged with its reasoning for audit and review.

This is how the product earns the right to act more autonomously over time: by building a track record its operators can see and trust.

docs.title: Open questions (for specs)
docs.text:
• How goals/objectives are expressed and weighted (single metric vs. multi-objective).
  • The experimentation framework (how holdouts are managed and measured).
  • Default autonomy levels per action type and how they're configured.
  • How conflicting recommendations across segments/goals are reconciled.

docs.title: Insights Engine
docs.text:
Pillar 2. Turns unified data and model outputs into custom insights — findings that are tailored, grounded, and decision-oriented.

An insight here is not a metric and not a chart. It is a claim about the business's customers, backed by evidence, that implies an action.

docs.title: What makes an insight "custom"
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T["Tailored<br/><small>this business, segment, customer</small>"] --> I((Custom<br/>Insight))
    G["Grounded<br/><small>traceable to data + reasoning</small>"] --> I
    D["Decision-oriented<br/><small>implies an action + impact</small>"] --> I

A finding earns the name only when all three hold. "Average order value is $48" is a metric. "Customers who buy accessories within 14 days of their first order have 2.3× the 12-month LTV, and 60% of first-time buyers never see an accessory offer" is an insight — tailored, grounded, and pointing at an action.

docs.title: Anatomy of an insight
docs.text: Field Meaning Statement The claim, in plain language. Evidence The data, segment, and model output behind it. Confidence How strongly the data supports it. Scope Which customers/segment it applies to and how many. Expected impact What acting on it is worth (e.g. estimated revenue/retention). Suggested decision The action it implies — handed to Decision Intelligence. Provenance The trace from raw data → reasoning → this statement.

docs.title: How insights are generated
docs.text:
The engine combines complementary methods rather than relying on one:

flowchart TB
    subgraph methods[Generation methods]
        ANOM[Anomaly / change detection]
        PATT[Pattern & correlation mining]
        COMP[Cohort & segment comparison]
        PRED[Model-driven<br/>propensities & drivers]
        LLM[LLM reasoning over<br/>evidence + context]
    end
    methods --> CAND[Candidate insights]
    CAND --> VALID[Validate against data]
    VALID --> RANK[Rank by expected value]
    RANK --> TOP[Surface top insights]
  • Anomaly / change detection — what moved, where, and for whom.
  • Pattern & correlation mining — recurring associations in behaviour.
  • Cohort & segment comparison — who differs from whom and why it matters.
  • Model-driven — propensities and their drivers from the behaviour models.
  • LLM reasoning — synthesizes evidence and business context into a plain-language, decision-framed statement; also proposes what to investigate next for the agent.

Guard against spurious findings

More methods means more candidate claims, and more chances for false positives. Every candidate is validated against the data (effect size, significance, holdout checks) before it is surfaced, and confidence is reported honestly.

docs.title: Ranking: value over volume
docs.text:
The engine's job is not to produce many insights but the right ones. Candidates are ranked by expected value of acting, roughly:

priority ≈ (impact if true) × (confidence) × (actionability) ÷ (effort/cost)

Low-confidence, low-impact, or un-actionable findings are suppressed. The agent can tune this ranking toward current goals (e.g. prioritize retention this quarter).

docs.title: Types of insight (illustrative)
docs.text: Type Example Opportunity "Segment X is under-offered product Y they're likely to want." Risk "These accounts show the early churn signature seen in past lapsers." Driver "Support response time is the strongest predictor of repeat purchase." Segment shift "A fast-growing new behavioural segment has emerged this month." Anomaly "Conversion for channel Z dropped 18% for mobile users only." Lifecycle "Customers stall at onboarding step 3; those who pass it retain 2×."

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• Pull: an operator asks a question in plain language; the engine answers with a grounded insight.
  • Push: the agent runs the engine continuously and surfaces high-value insights without being asked.

Both paths produce the same structured insight object, so everything is explainable and feeds Decision Intelligence identically.

docs.title: Open questions (for specs)
docs.text:
• The exact validation/statistical bar before surfacing.
  • How business context and goals are encoded for the LLM reasoning step.
  • De-duplication and "insight fatigue" controls (not re-surfacing known findings).
  • How confidence is calibrated and communicated.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Businesses generate more customer signal than ever, and act on less of it than they think. Three gaps recur:

docs.title: 1. Data is fragmented
docs.text:
Customer information lives in separate systems that rarely agree on who a customer is or what they did:

flowchart LR
    A[E-commerce / POS] -.no shared ID.-> X((?))
    B[CRM] -.no shared ID.-> X
    C[Web & app analytics] -.no shared ID.-> X
    D[Support desk] -.no shared ID.-> X
    E[Email / ads platforms] -.no shared ID.-> X
    X[/"Who is this customer,<br/>really?"/]

The same person is a row in the POS, a contact in the CRM, an anonymous device in analytics, and a ticket in support — with nothing tying them together.

docs.title: 2. Insight is reactive and manual
docs.text: Even where data is joined, the standard tool is a dashboard: it shows metrics and waits for a human to notice something, form a hypothesis, and go dig. The questions asked are limited by the analyst's time and imagination, and most patterns are never looked for.

docs.title: 3. Insight rarely becomes a decision
docs.text: The last mile is the hardest. A chart showing churn rising does not, by itself, tell anyone which customers, why, or what to do. The translation from "interesting finding" to "specific action taken" is where most value leaks out.

docs.title: Why now
docs.text:
• Agentic AI is viable. LLM-based agents can plan, use tools, query data, and explain their reasoning — making an "analyst that works on its own" realistic rather than aspirational.
  • Customer data is more connectable. Modern data stacks (warehouses, CDPs, event pipelines) make integration tractable where it used to be bespoke.
  • Expectations have shifted. Customers expect relevance; businesses expect their tools to be proactive. Static reporting no longer meets either.

docs.title: Who it's for
docs.text: Audience Pain today What AutoAgentAI gives them Growth / marketing teams Segments go stale; targeting is coarse Live, behaviour-based segments and next-best-action per customer Product teams Hard to see how usage predicts retention or expansion Behaviour models linking usage to outcomes Customer success / retention Churn noticed too late Early, explained churn risk with recommended saves Analysts / data teams Flooded with ad-hoc requests An agent that handles the routine slicing and surfaces the non-obvious Leadership Decisions made on gut or lagging reports Decision-ready insight tied to measurable outcomes

docs.title: The core bet
docs.text:
If an autonomous agent integrates the customer data, continuously generates insight tailored to the business, and frames every insight as a decision, then businesses act on far more of their signal — and the gap between "data we have" and "decisions we make" closes.

This is the thesis the rest of the documentation builds on. The architecture is the structure designed to deliver it; the use cases make it concrete.

A phased path from concept and documentation (where the project is now) to a validated product. Phases are about proving the next risky thing, not calendar dates.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Concrete scenarios that make the pillars tangible. Each follows the same arc: integrate → model → insight → decision → outcome.

docs.title: 1. E-commerce: rescue a silently churning cohort
docs.text:
Situation. An online retailer's repeat-purchase rate is slipping, but the headline numbers look fine.

flowchart LR
    A[Integrate orders,<br/>web events, email] --> B[Behaviour models:<br/>churn risk + RFM]
    B --> C["Insight: a high-LTV cohort<br/>stopped browsing 3 wks<br/>before they stop buying"]
    C --> D["Decision: win-back offer<br/>to the cohort, pre-lapse"]
    D --> E[Outcome: reactivation<br/>measured vs. holdout]
  • Insight: customers who were worth the most show a 3-week engagement drop before their purchases stop — a leading indicator no dashboard was tracking.
  • Decision: the agent proposes a targeted, time-boxed win-back to exactly those accounts, before they lapse.
  • Outcome: reactivation rate measured against a holdout; what works feeds the next round.

docs.title: 2. SaaS: turn usage signals into expansion
docs.text:
Situation. A B2B SaaS wants to grow existing accounts but can't tell which are ready.

  • Integrate: product usage events + CRM + billing.
  • Model: feature-adoption depth, engagement trend, expansion propensity.
  • Insight: accounts that adopt feature X within 30 days expand at 3× the rate; a set of current accounts just crossed that threshold.
  • Decision: flag those accounts to sales with the evidence and a suggested expansion play; nudge stalled accounts toward feature X.
  • Outcome: expansion revenue attributed to flagged vs. unflagged accounts.

docs.title: 3. Subscription / DTC: reduce involuntary and voluntary churn
docs.text:
• Integrate: subscriptions, payments, support, app usage.
  • Model: churn risk split by cause (price, dunning/failed payment, dissatisfaction, low usage).
  • Insight: a third of churn is involuntary (failed payments), not a loyalty problem at all.
  • Decision: route involuntary-risk customers to smart dunning; route dissatisfaction-risk to a save play; leave content customers alone.
  • Outcome: churn reduction by cause, each measured separately.

docs.title: 4. Retail / omnichannel: unify online + in-store, then personalize
docs.text:
• Integrate: POS + e-commerce + loyalty, resolved to one customer.
  • Model: cross-channel behaviour, product affinity, channel preference.
  • Insight: customers who shop both channels are worth 2× single-channel ones, and a large single-channel group looks ready to cross over.
  • Decision: encourage the cross-over with channel-appropriate, affinity-based offers.
  • Outcome: cross-channel conversion and LTV lift.

docs.title: 5. Plain-language investigation (pull mode)
docs.text:
Not every use case is automated. An operator can simply ask:

"Why did conversion drop last week?"

The agent perceives the question, queries the integrated data, compares cohorts, and returns a grounded insight — "the drop is isolated to mobile users on channel Z after the checkout change on the 12th; desktop is flat" — with the evidence and a suggested next step. Same machinery, human-initiated.

docs.title: Pattern across all use cases
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I[Integrate the data] --> M[Model the behaviour]
    M --> N[Surface the insight] --> D[Frame the decision]
    D --> A[Act within guardrails] --> O[Measure the outcome]
    O -.learn.-> M

The value isn't any single model or chart — it's an autonomous loop that keeps finding the non-obvious and tying it to a decision, across the whole customer base, continuously.

These are illustrative

Numbers and scenarios here are examples to convey the shape of the product, not claims or benchmarks. Real validation comes with the roadmap.

docs.title: The title, decoded
docs.text:
The project's full name is a compact specification. Read left to right:

AutoAgent · and Customer-Integrated · Custom Insights · into Purchase · and Overall Behaviour · and Decision Making.

  • AutoAgent — the system is an autonomous agent. It has goals, it acts on its own cadence, and it decides what question to ask next instead of waiting to be queried.
  • Customer-Integrated — it is wired into the business's customer data and systems. Insights are grounded in this business's customers, not a generic model.
  • Custom Insights — output is tailored: specific to the business, the segment, and often the individual customer.
  • into Purchase — a first-class focus on buying behaviour: conversion, basket, frequency, value, churn.
  • and Overall Behaviour — the whole customer relationship: engagement, usage, support interactions, sentiment, lifecycle stage.
  • and Decision Making — insights exist to drive decisions — the agent frames findings as actions a human or system can take, and can take some itself.

docs.title: Vision statement
docs.text: Every business should have an analyst that never sleeps, never forgets a customer, and always ties what it finds to a decision. AutoAgentAI is that analyst as an autonomous agent — it reads all the customer signal a business generates, learns how its customers buy and behave, and continuously turns that into decisions that grow the relationship.

docs.title: What success looks like
docs.text:
For the businessFor the operator (analyst / marketer / ops)For the customer (end result)
  • A single, trustworthy, resolved view of each customer.
  • A steady stream of decisions, not just charts: "offer X to segment Y," "these 300 accounts are about to churn — here's why and what to do."
  • Measurably better outcomes: higher conversion, retention, and lifetime value, with the agent's contribution attributable.
  • Hours of manual slicing-and-dicing replaced by reviewing and approving agent-proposed actions.
  • Ability to ask the agent questions in plain language and get grounded answers.
  • Trust: every insight traces back to the data and reasoning behind it.
  • More relevant offers and less noise.
  • Problems anticipated before they become complaints.
  • A relationship that feels understood rather than mass-marketed to.

docs.title: Guiding principles
docs.text:
1. Decision-first. An insight that doesn't change a decision is noise. Every output is framed as "so what should we do?"
  2. Grounded and explainable. Every insight traces to the data and reasoning that produced it. No black-box pronouncements.
  3. Autonomous but accountable. The agent acts on its own cadence, but within guardrails, with human-in-the-loop where stakes are high, and with a full audit trail.
  4. Custom over generic. Models and insights adapt to each business; the product is not a one-size-fits-all benchmark report.
  5. Privacy and trust by design. Customer data is sensitive; consent, minimization, and security are foundations, not afterthoughts.

docs.title: Non-goals (for now)
docs.text:
• Not a general-purpose BI tool — it is opinionated toward customer behaviour and decisions.
  • Not a data warehouse — it integrates with and reads from existing stores rather than replacing them.
  • Not a fully hands-off autopilot on day one — autonomy is earned progressively as trust and guardrails mature (see the roadmap).

This framing is a draft

The decoding above is the current working interpretation of the project name. If the intended meaning differs, this page is the right place to correct it — everything else in the docs follows from here.

docs.title: AutoAgentAI — For Sales Managers
docs.text:
Straight talk, no tech jargon. Here's what this thing actually does for your store.

In plain English

It's a smart assistant that quietly watches every customer — online, on the lot, in service — remembers everything, and tells your people exactly who to call, what they care about, and how to help them buy. It never forgets a lead, and it runs on a box in your back office, so your customer info never leaves the building.

docs.title: The problem you already know
docs.text:
• Leads fall through the cracks. Somebody gets busy, forgets to follow up, and that deal walks to the store down the road.
  • Your best closers keep it all in their head. When they leave, it walks out with them.
  • Half the real story never gets written down — the customer who loved the SUV but worried about gas money, the trade-in that's about to die. Your people can't sell and type notes at the same time, so they (rightly) stay present and the details vanish.
  • You find out why you lost a deal... never. You just see the number at month-end.

None of that is your people being lazy. It's impossible for a human to track every customer across the website, the showroom, the phone, and service all at once. A computer can. That's the whole idea.

docs.title: What it does for your store
docs.text: What you want How it helps Stop losing leads It tracks every customer automatically and tells your rep who to follow up with, today, and why. Know your customer before you walk up "This is Maria — second kid coming, loved the hybrid, worried about running costs, her current car's on its last legs." On your rep's iPad, before hello. Sell more, without pressure Your rep leads with the answer to the customer's real worry instead of a generic pitch. People buy when they feel understood. Catch more trade-ins It spots when someone's car is near the end and flags it. Keep service customers coming back It notices who's drifting and nudges before they're gone. Never lose the knowledge When a rep leaves, everything they knew about every customer stays in the system.

docs.title: What your salespeople's day looks like
docs.text:
• They carry an iPad. It's their window into the whole system — anywhere on the lot.
  • Customers can use self-serve kiosks (like the ones at McDonald's) — easy, no-pressure, and they quietly tell the system what the customer's interested in.
  • Instead of guessing who to chase, your rep opens the iPad and sees a short list: these customers, this is what they need, here's what to say.
  • The boring admin — logging notes, remembering follow-ups — the system does it.

docs.title: "Is this going to replace my salespeople?"
docs.text:
Honest answer: it changes the job more than it replaces people.

  • The parts that go away are the parts nobody liked anyway — chasing, guessing, and data entry.
  • The part that stays and matters more is the human part: making a nervous buyer feel taken care of. The computer can't do that. Your people can.
  • You'll likely run a leaner, sharper team where each person handles more customers and gives each one more attention, because the busywork is gone. Your closers become trusted advisors, not pressure salesmen.

Think of it as giving every salesperson a tireless assistant who remembers everything and does the paperwork.

docs.title: Your info stays yours
docs.text:
This runs on a computer in your dealership. Your customers' names, numbers, and details don't get shipped off to some cloud company. That keeps you on the right side of privacy laws and lets you tell customers, honestly, "your information stays here with us." (More on that if you care: the privacy page.)

You can start cheap and simple to try it out, then move to the in-house setup once you see it working. Four options, from a low-cost trial to a full in-store system — the four setups.

docs.title: What you have to do
docs.text:
Not much. The system does the watching, remembering, and suggesting. Your job stays the same: lead a team that takes great care of customers — just with way better information and nothing falling through the cracks.

The bottom line

Every customer tracked. No lead lost. Your reps walk up already knowing what matters. More sales, more trade-ins, more repeat service — and your customer info never leaves the building.

Want to see how one customer goes from "just looking" to "sold"? Read the quick story: From Raw Data to a Decision.

docs.title: AutoAgentAI — Investor Pitch
docs.text:
The one-liner

AutoAgentAI is an autonomous AI agent that captures and uses the most valuable, least-captured data in the car industry — the buyer's real pre-purchase intent and decision behaviour — running privately on-prem so it clears the privacy bar that kills everyone else, and closing the loop from the showroom floor all the way to the OEM.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The automotive purchase is one of the largest, most considered, most emotional consumer decisions there is — and the data about why buyers choose, hesitate, and walk is almost entirely uncaptured. Not under-captured: structurally uncapturable, because the only people positioned to capture it — salespeople — can't (why). The industry runs on memory, sticky notes, lagging sales figures, and survey-with-a-prize-draw guesswork.

docs.title: Why now
docs.text:
Three curves crossed at the same time:

flowchart LR
    A["Agentic AI matured<br/><small>autonomous capture + reasoning</small>"] --> NOW((The opening))
    B["Open local models got good enough<br/><small>private, on-prem, cheap inference</small>"] --> NOW
    C["Privacy law tightening<br/><small>sovereign data is the only durable posture</small>"] --> NOW

For the first time it is possible to capture this data (agentic AI), do it privately (local models on-prem), and act on it autonomously — all at once. That simultaneity is the window.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
An autonomous agent across four capabilities — unify the dealership's customer data, model behaviour, generate custom insights, and turn them into decisions and actions — delivered through McDonald's-style kiosks and iPad nodes on the floor, and running entirely on the dealership's own hardware.

See the architecture and the raw-data-to-action scenario.

docs.title: The wedge: the most valuable data in autos
docs.text:
Value = stakes × relationship length × decision-signal × scarcity × reach up the chain. This data scores at the top of all five (detail):

  • Huge stakes per decision — a vehicle, a trade-in, finance, years of service.
  • A lifelong, repeating relationship — shop → buy → own → service → trade → repeat.
  • Genuine decision signal, not vanity metrics.
  • Scarce — basically nobody has it, because it was uncapturable.
  • Valuable at every level — salesperson, dealer, group, and OEM.

docs.title: The moat
docs.text:
The AI is commodity. The moat is capture + privacy + the loop:

Layer Why it defends Data capture Being in every channel at once, capturing as a by-product — hard to replicate without the on-floor footprint On-prem/private The only posture that can legally hold this PII at scale as law tightens (privacy) The OEM loop Once aggregated buyer-intent flows to manufacturers and shapes product/pricing, it compounds and entrenches (loop) Data network effect Every interaction sharpens the models; more dealers → more signal → better product

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T0["Tier 0 · Cloud<br/><small>low-cost pilot / land</small>"] --> T1["Tier 1 · Local Essentials"]
    T1 --> T2["Tier 2 · Local Pro"]
    T2 --> T3["Tier 3 · Enterprise / Group"]
  • Land with low-cost Tier 0 pilots to prove value fast.
  • Expand to on-prem Tiers 1–3 (hardware + license/subscription) once proven — the identical workflows migrate with no rebuild.
  • Multiply across a dealer group (Tier 3) and, longer term, monetize the aggregated OEM feedback loop — a second revenue surface the data unlocks.

Revenue surfaces: setup/hardware, recurring license per site/seat, group/enterprise contracts, and OEM-facing insight products.

docs.title: Market
docs.text:
Tens of thousands of dealerships; a global new+used vehicle market measured in the trillions; OEMs that spend heavily to infer buyer intent they could instead measure. The beachhead is a single rooftop; the expansion is the group; the prize is the loop to the manufacturer.

On numbers

Market and revenue framing here is directional for positioning. A bottoms-up model (per-rooftop economics, attach rates, hardware vs. recurring split) is a fast-follow once a design-partner dealer is signed.

docs.title: Go-to-market
docs.text:
1. Design-partner dealership — Tier 0/1, prove conversion, trade-in capture, and retention lift against a holdout.
  2. Reference rooftop → group — expand within the group on Tiers 2/3.
  3. OEM conversation — bring aggregated, anonymized buyer-intent signal to the manufacturer; open the loop revenue.

docs.title: Roadmap & the ask
docs.text:
Today: concept and documentation complete (roadmap). Next: specifications and a design-partner pilot. The ask: [capital / a design-partner dealer / an OEM introduction — fill in per conversation] to fund Phase 1 (specs) and a measured Tier-0/1 pilot that proves the lift and the loop.

Why we win

Everyone has an AI agent. We found the gold it's for — the car industry's most valuable data — and we're the only ones capturing it privately and closing the loop to the OEM. The technology is ordinary; the position is not.

docs.title: AutoAgentAI — Technical Overview
docs.text:
A dense, engineer-facing tour for someone evaluating how it's built and whether it holds up. For the full treatment, follow the links into the detailed docs.

System in one sentence

A stateful, autonomous agent orchestrates four capability pillars — data integration, behaviour modeling, insight generation, and decision intelligence — over a dealership's unified customer data, running on local open-source models, on-prem, behind thin kiosk/iPad clients.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Four pillars in a pipeline, driven by a fifth (the agent). Full detail: Architecture.

        CIL["Customer Integration<br/><small>ingest · resolve · enrich · store</small>"]
    end
    subgraph intel[Intelligence layer]

        DI[Decision Intelligence]
    end
    AG(["AutoAgent<br/><small>plan · tools · memory · guardrails</small>"])
    SRC[Dealer systems] --> CIL --> BM --> IE --> DI --> OUT[Insights / actions]
    AG -.orchestrates.-> CIL & BM & IE & DI
    OUT -.outcomes.-> AG
Layer Responsibility Detail Source Dealer systems: DMS/CRM, web, service, finance — Data Ingest, identity resolution, enrichment, unified profiles Customer Integration Intelligence Propensities, segments, insights, next-best-action Models · Insights · Decisions Agent Orchestration, memory, autonomy, audit Agent Loop Experience Kiosks, iPad nodes, approvals, chat, API Hardware

docs.title: Deployment topology
docs.text:
Thin clients, intelligent core. Kiosks and iPads are nodes, not stores — models and data stay on the on-prem box.

flowchart TB
    subgraph node[On-prem node / cluster]
        M[Local models<br/>GPU inference]
        VS[(Vector store /<br/>knowledge base)]

    end

    IP[iPad nodes] --- node
    node -. aggregated, consented .-> OEM[OEM / group sync]

Four tiers scale the same stack from a single workstation (Tier 1) to a redundant GPU cluster (Tier 3); Tier 0 is a cloud variant for non-sensitive pilots. See the tier matrix.

docs.title: Local model strategy
docs.text:
Tasks are bounded — read, extract, classify, summarize, rank, draft — and retrieval-grounded + structured-output-constrained, which is precisely where open local models match cloud models. Rationale and limits: Local Models Are Enough.

  • Grounding: RAG over the local knowledge base; the model reasons over supplied facts, not parametric memory.
  • Structure: schema-constrained outputs (fill fields, pick from menus) over freeform generation.
  • Decomposition: multi-step logic lives in the agent/tools, not one giant call; each inference is small and verifiable.
  • Economics: fixed-cost inference enables a continuously-running loop without a per-call meter.

docs.title: Data model & identity
docs.text: Conceptual model (physical schema deferred to specs): a Customer with many Identity, Event, Order, Interaction, and Feature records. Identity resolution is deterministic-first (strong keys), probabilistic with confidence scoring for the rest, and confidence-aware (low-confidence links are flagged, not silently merged). Detail: Customer Integration.

docs.title: Agent runtime
docs.text: Perceive → reason/plan → act → learn, on its own cadence (scheduled + event-driven). Three memory types (working, episodic, semantic). Tools = the four pillars + dealer systems. Detail: Agent Loop.

docs.title: Security, privacy & guardrails
docs.text:
• Data locality is the primary control: on-prem means no third-party processors, no cross-border transfer, minimal breach surface (privacy).
  • Guardrails: graduated autonomy L0–L4; confidence floors; budget/frequency caps; excluded actions; escalation.
  • Provenance: every insight/action carries a trace (data → reasoning → output) for explainability and audit of automated decisions.
  • Safety: reversible actions, kill-switch, external text treated as data not instructions.
  • Thin clients: a lost iPad is a window, not a database copy.

docs.title: What's decided vs. deferred
docs.text:
Decided (logical) Deferred to Phase-1 specs (physical) Five-pillar architecture; on-prem-first; thin clients Concrete stack, languages, datastores Local-model-first; retrieval-grounded; structured outputs Specific model(s), GPU sizing, eval bar Graduated autonomy + provenance Default guardrail envelopes, action catalog v1 Conceptual data model Physical schema, ingestion (stream vs batch)

Deliberately logical-first so the concept isn't prematurely locked to a stack; ADRs capture load-bearing choices when specs begin. See Specifications and the Roadmap.

Evaluation is a first-class Phase-1 deliverable

A task-level eval suite on real dealership data proves the chosen local model clears the quality bar before anything ships — the claim in Local Models Are Enough is to be measured, not asserted.

docs.title: Cloud vs On-Prem: The Risks
docs.text:
Tier 0 (cloud AI services + cloud storage) is cheap, fast, and genuinely works — and for sensitive customer data it carries risks that on-prem simply removes. This page lays the two side by side so the trade-off is made with eyes open, not by default.

The one-sentence version

With cloud AI you are renting someone else's computer to hold and read your most valuable, most regulated data; with on-prem you own the box, the model, and the risk surface — and the data never leaves.

docs.title: Where the risk actually lives
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph cloud[Cloud AI path]
      C1[Your customer data] --> C2[Network egress]
      C2 --> C3[Vendor cloud]
      C3 --> C4[AI provider]
      C4 --> C5[Sub-processors / regions]
    end
    subgraph onprem[On-prem path]
      O1[Your customer data] --> O2[Local node]
      O2 --> O1
    end
    cloud -.-> RISK["Each hop = exposure,<br/>dependency, obligation"]
    onprem -.-> SAFE["One box you control"]

Every arrow leaving your building is a place where data can be exposed, retained, subpoenaed, repriced, or quietly used for something you didn't intend.

docs.title: The risks of cloud AI for this data
docs.text: Risk What it means for a dealership Data leaves your control Customer PII, finances, and behaviour sit on infrastructure you don't own and can't fully inspect. Secondary use / training Depending on terms, prompts and data may be logged, retained, or used to improve vendor models. Terms can change. Vendor lock-in & pricing power Your workflows depend on an API someone else prices, throttles, deprecates, or changes. Availability dependence An outage or a suspended account at the provider takes your showroom tools down with it. Breach surface A breach anywhere in the vendor → AI-provider → sub-processor chain can expose your customers, and it's your name on the apology. Compliance drag Processor agreements, transfer mechanisms, audits, and disclosures — ongoing paperwork and liability for every vendor in the chain. Cross-border exposure Data may be processed in regions whose laws (and access powers) differ from yours. Loss of provenance Harder to prove why an automated decision was made when the reasoning happened in a black-box API. Confidential leakage Your competitive edge — how you sell, what works — flows through a third party.

docs.title: The risks on-prem removes (and the ones it adds)
docs.text:
Removed or sharply reduced: data leaving the premises, secondary use by a vendor, cross-border transfer, dependence on a provider's pricing/uptime/terms, and most of the processor-chain compliance drag.

Added (and manageable):

On-prem cost Mitigation Upfront hardware (capex) Scoped by tier; amortizes against avoided per-call cloud fees and risk You run the box Managed appliance model, updates, and support; thin kiosks/iPads keep it simple You own uptime UPS, and HA/redundancy at Tier 3 Model updates are yours to apply Open models are swappable; updates are a controlled, local step

On-prem trades a recurring, external, hard-to-bound risk (someone else holds your data) for a one-time, internal, boundable cost (you run a server). For data this sensitive, that trade usually favors on-prem.

docs.title: When cloud (Tier 0) is still the right call
docs.text:
Tier 0 is not wrong — it's wrong for sensitive data. It's a good fit when:

  • You're running a pilot or demo to prove value before buying hardware.
  • The workload uses non-sensitive or synthetic data.
  • You explicitly accept the posture for a bounded, short-lived purpose.

The product is designed so you can start on Tier 0 and migrate the identical workflows on-prem once value is proven — no rebuild. See On-Prem AI & Hardware.

docs.title: The decision, framed
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Q{Is this real,<br/>regulated customer data?}
    Q -->|No / pilot / synthetic| CLOUD[Tier 0 cloud is fine<br/>cheap, fast]
    Q -->|Yes| LOCAL{How much scale<br/>and uptime?}
    LOCAL -->|One site, starting| T1[Tier 1 Local Essentials]
    LOCAL -->|Full dealership| T2[Tier 2 Local Pro]
    LOCAL -->|Group / multi-site| T3[Tier 3 Local Enterprise]

The asymmetry that matters

A cloud cost saving is visible and small each month. A privacy failure with customer PII is invisible until it isn't, and then it is large, public, and permanent. The risks are not symmetric — which is why, for this data, the default recommendation is on-prem. See Privacy, PII & Future-Proofing.

docs.title: Local Models Are Enough
docs.text:
Thesis: for the specific jobs AutoAgentAI needs an AI model to do, today's open-source local models do the work as well as the big cloud models — well enough that giving up the cloud costs you nothing that matters, and buys you everything on the privacy and risk pages.

Why this is true now and wasn't before

The gap between frontier cloud models and the best open models has narrowed to the point where, on bounded, well-scoped tasks, they are interchangeable. Our tasks are exactly that kind — bounded and well-scoped — not open-ended frontier reasoning. You don't need the world's biggest model to read a sales note.

docs.title: What the model actually has to do here
docs.text:
The agent doesn't need a model that can do everything. It needs a model that can do these things, reliably, on dealership data:

Job What it looks like Difficulty for a local model Read & understand notes, messages, reviews "Customer worried about resale value, has two kids" Easy — well within local models Extract structure from free text Pull intent, budget signals, objections into fields Easy / moderate Classify & tag Intent, sentiment, lifecycle stage, segment Easy Summarize Condense a visit or a history into a brief Easy Rank & choose Next-best-action from a known menu Moderate — and aided by the models in Behaviour Models Draft language A friendly follow-up, a kiosk prompt Easy Reason over retrieved facts Answer grounded in the local knowledge base Moderate — handled well with retrieval

None of these is a frontier task. They are the bread-and-butter capabilities that even modest open models now handle, especially when grounded in retrieval (the model reasons over your facts rather than from memory) and constrained to structured outputs (it fills fields, not freeform essays).

docs.title: Why scoped tasks favor local models
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    FRONTIER["Open-ended frontier reasoning<br/><small>where the biggest cloud models still lead</small>"]
    OURS["Bounded, grounded, structured tasks<br/><small>read · extract · classify · rank · draft</small>"]
    FRONTIER -.-> GAP[Big model advantage]
    OURS -.-> NOGAP[Little to no practical advantage]

Three design choices shrink the model's burden until a local one is plenty:

  1. Retrieval-grounded. The knowledge lives in the local knowledge base; the model reads from it instead of recalling. This leans on comprehension, which local models are good at — not on a giant parametric memory.
  2. Structured outputs. The agent asks the model to populate fields and pick from menus, not to free-associate. Constrained tasks are where small models are most reliable.
  3. The agent does the planning. Multi-step logic lives in the agent loop and the deterministic tools — not in one giant model call. Each model call is small and well-defined.

docs.title: Honest limits and how we handle them
docs.text:
Being truthful about where local models are weaker, and the mitigations:

Limitation Mitigation Hardest open-ended reasoning lags frontier models We don't route such tasks to the model; the agent decomposes them Smaller models hallucinate more when ungrounded Retrieval-grounding + "answer only from provided facts" + provenance checks Throughput is bounded by your GPU Tier sizing (hardware); batch non-interactive work Occasional task needs more horsepower Optional: a larger local model at Tier 2/3, or an explicit, consented, non-PII cloud call for that one task

docs.title: The economics flip, too
docs.text:
Cloud models charge per call, forever, and the bill grows with success. A local model is a fixed cost you've already paid: once the hardware is in, inference is effectively free and unlimited, which changes how the agent can behave — it can afford to be continuously curious (the whole point of an autonomous agent) without a meter running on every thought.

Cloud models Local models Cost shape Per-call, recurring, scales with use Fixed capex, then ~free inference "Always-on curiosity" Expensive — every loop costs money Cheap — run the loop as often as you like Data exposure Leaves premises Stays on premises Dependency Vendor terms/pricing/uptime Yours

docs.title: The conclusion
docs.text:
For AutoAgentAI's actual workload — reading, extracting, classifying, summarizing, ranking, and drafting over a dealership's own grounded data — a local open-source model does the job as well as a cloud model, at a fixed cost, with the data never leaving the building. The cloud's remaining edge is in open-ended frontier reasoning the agent is designed not to depend on.

That is what makes the on-prem tiers not a compromise but the better engineering choice for this problem.

Claims here are directional

Specific model choices and measured quality bars are a Phase-1 specification task — including the evaluation suite that proves, on real dealership tasks, that the chosen local model clears the bar.

docs.title: On-Prem, Local AI & Hardware
docs.text:
AutoAgentAI is built so it can run entirely on the dealership's own premises, on local hardware, with local AI models, so that customer data never leaves the building. This is not a bolt-on — it is a first-class deployment mode, and for most dealerships it is the recommended one, because the data involved is exactly the kind that privacy law treats as sensitive (see Privacy, PII & Future-Proofing).

The core promise

Everything the agent needs — the models that read and reason, the knowledge base, the customer data, the decision-making — can live on a machine in the back office. The only things that cross the network are the things you explicitly choose to send out (e.g. a manufacturer feedback summary), and even those are on your terms.

docs.title: Why on-prem is now realistic
docs.text:
Two things changed:

  1. Open-source local models got good enough. The open models you can run on a single workstation today do the specific jobs this product needs — reading notes, classifying intent, summarizing, extracting structure, ranking options, drafting language — at a quality that was cloud-only a short time ago. See Local Models Are Enough.
  2. Agentic AI matured. The orchestration, tool-use, and memory patterns that make an autonomous agent work no longer require a frontier cloud model for every step. The heavy reasoning can be reserved, batched, or done locally.

Together, these make a fully local, private, autonomous customer-intelligence agent buildable on dealership hardware — which a few years ago it was not.

docs.title: The four deployment options
docs.text:
AutoAgentAI ships as four tiers, from cheapest-but-not-private to fully sovereign. A dealer picks based on how sensitive their data is, what they can spend, and how much they want to keep in-house.

    T1["Tier 1 · Local Essentials<br/><small>one on-prem node<br/>small local models</small>"]
    T2["Tier 2 · Local Pro<br/><small>GPU server<br/>mid/large local models</small>"]
    T3["Tier 3 · Local Enterprise<br/><small>GPU cluster · HA<br/>group / multi-site</small>"]
    T0 --> T1 --> T2 --> T3
    T0 -. "data leaves premises" .-> X["⚠ not PII-compliant<br/>for sensitive data"]
    T1 --- P["🔒 data never leaves"]
    T2 --- P
    T3 --- P
Tier 0 — Cloud Tier 1 — Local Essentials Tier 2 — Local Pro Tier 3 — Local Enterprise AI Cloud AI services Small/mid local models Mid/large local models Largest local models, redundant Storage Cloud On-prem On-prem On-prem, replicated Hardware None / minimal One mini-server or workstation GPU server/workstation GPU cluster, HA, UPS Data location Third-party cloud On premises On premises On premises (sovereign) PII-law posture ⚠ Not compliant for sensitive data Compliant Compliant Compliant + auditable at scale Cost Lowest upfront Low Moderate (capex) Highest (capex) Best for Pilots, low-sensitivity, proof-of-value Single rooftop, getting started privately A full dealership operation Dealer groups, flagship, multi-site Scale Elastic 1 site, light load 1 site, full load, many nodes Many sites, high concurrency

docs.title: Tier 0 — Cloud (cheap, fast, not PII-compliant)
docs.text: Uses cloud AI services and cloud storage. No or minimal on-site hardware. It is the cheapest and quickest way to stand the system up and prove it works — and it can genuinely work. The catch is unavoidable: customer data leaves the premises and passes through third-party cloud and AI providers, so it is not suitable for PII-regulated customer data. Use it for pilots, demos, non-sensitive workloads, or proving value before investing in hardware — with eyes open about the trade-off (see Cloud vs On-Prem: The Risks).

docs.title: Tier 1 — Local Essentials (entry on-prem, private)
docs.text: A single on-prem node — a capable mini-server or workstation — runs small-to-mid local models and holds the data locally. Data never leaves the building. Modest cost, modest footprint; ideal for a single rooftop that wants privacy from day one and a real but contained workload.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Local Pro (dealership-grade, private)
docs.text: A proper on-prem GPU server/workstation runs mid-to-large local models with a local knowledge base and vector store, driving a full fleet of kiosks and iPads across the dealership. Handles the real concurrent load of a busy showroom. This is the sweet spot for most single dealerships that take their data seriously.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Local Enterprise (group / flagship, sovereign)
docs.text:
A GPU cluster with high availability, redundancy, and the largest local models, serving a dealer group or multiple sites. Data sovereignty across the whole group, auditable at scale, with edge-sync between locations. For organizations where the data is strategic and downtime is unacceptable.

Same product, different engine

All four tiers run the same AutoAgentAI — same pillars, same interfaces, same agent. What changes is where the compute and data live and how much of it you can run at once. A dealer can start at Tier 0 to prove value, then move the exact same workflows on-prem at Tier 1–3 when ready.

docs.title: Interfaces: kiosks and iPads
docs.text:
The system meets people where they are, with two complementary interfaces:

  • McDonald's-style self-serve kiosks. Large, friendly, touch-first terminals — the same pattern customers already trust from quick-service restaurants. Low intimidation, self-paced, and they capture rich interaction data as a natural by-product of being genuinely useful to the customer.
  • iPads. The mobile, handheld form of the same system. Crucially, iPads are generally the nodes that connect to the whole system — a salesperson or greeter carries one, and through it the whole local AutoAgentAI (models, data, agent) is at hand anywhere on the lot or in the showroom.
flowchart TB
    subgraph onprem[On-prem AutoAgentAI node]
        M[Local AI models]
        KB[(Local knowledge base<br/>+ customer data)]
        AG[AutoAgent]
        M --- AG
        KB --- AG
    end
    K1[Kiosk] --- onprem
    K2[Kiosk] --- onprem
    IP1[iPad node] --- onprem
    IP2[iPad node] --- onprem
    IP3[iPad node] --- onprem
    onprem -. "only chosen,<br/>aggregated outputs" .-> OEM[OEM / HQ feedback]

The iPads and kiosks are thin — the intelligence and the data stay on the on-prem node. A lost or stolen iPad carries no customer database; it is a window into the local system, not a copy of it.

docs.title: What a local deployment contains
docs.text: Component Role Lives where Local AI models Reading, reasoning, extraction, drafting, ranking On-prem node (GPU) Knowledge base / vector store The dealership's customers, vehicles, history On-prem storage Unified customer profiles The resolved view per customer On-prem storage AutoAgent runtime Orchestration, memory, guardrails On-prem node Kiosk + iPad apps Thin interfaces / nodes Devices on the LAN Outbound (optional, chosen) Aggregated OEM feedback, group sync Egress on your terms

docs.title: Hardware guidance (illustrative)
docs.text:
Exact specifications are a Phase-1 spec decision and depend on chosen models and load. As rough orientation only:

  • Tier 1: a single modern workstation with one capable GPU and ample RAM/SSD — enough for small/mid local models and a single site's light, interactive load.
  • Tier 2: a dedicated GPU server (one or more workstation/data-center GPUs), fast NVMe storage, and a UPS — enough for larger models and a showroom's full concurrent kiosk + iPad load.
  • Tier 3: multiple GPU servers in a rack with redundancy, high-availability, and replicated storage — for dealer-group scale and uptime guarantees.

Numbers here are orientation, not a quote

Treat all hardware and cost statements as directional. Final sizing comes with the specifications once models and expected load are fixed.
